newsitem.title: UK: IPE gas futures start Jan after frustrating delay.
newsitem.headline: IPE gas futures start Jan after frustrating delay.

text.p: A long-awaited natural gas futures contract will start trading on the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on January 31, 1997 after months of frustrating delay.

Richard Ward, business development director at the IPE, told Reuters on Wednesday that natural gas futures had been under investigation since he joined the exchange in March 1995, and had been actively worked on for the whole of this year.

It was only after receiving approval from the board of the IPE, the board of the London Clearing House (LCH) -- which will technically be the counterparty in every contract traded on the exchange -- and, most importantly, from industry regulator Ofgas, that the IPE was able to announce a start-up date.

Ward is in no doubt of the need for a futures contract. "The industry has developed quickly to the point where it would benefit from a standardised instrument trading in a transparent manner with all the advantages of guarantees and anonymity that we offer".
He added that the time is now right because following fairly dramatic developments over the past two years, there is now an active spot market in the UK.

Ward believes that on an average day, around 150 million therms of gas are traded on the over-the-counter spot market in Britain - with spot in this context usually taken to mean up to one year forward. This is based on reporting services recording around 50 million therms of trade each day, and Ward estimates that they capture around one third of the total volumes traded.

"So on an average day the spot market is around twice the size of the whole physical gas market. But on record days reporting services show around 250 million therms of traded gas, indicating that on those days the spot market is eight times the size of the gas market".

NYMEX's natural gas contract, launched in 1990, now trades 35,000 lots, or 3.5 billion therms, a day, making it the third largest energy futures contract in the world and the most successful derivatives contract launched this decade.

But Ward does not anticipate such developments on the IPE. "I would love it if we could follow the U.S. model, but we need to be realistic. The U.S. market is 10 times the size of the market in the U.K., and there are many more shippers and traders there".
But this may change, he feels, when the Interconnector, carrying 20 billion cubic metres a year of gas from Bacton in Norfolk to Zeebrugge in Belgium, opens in October 1998.

"The Interconnector will have a positive impact from a market perspective on the European market. It will make Bacton more of a benchmark for pricing and it will see gas from the U.K. Continental Shelf sold on the European market. We already have gas to gas competition in the U.K. and we will start to see it elsewhere".

He added that growth of the market in Europe still depends heavily on the European Union's gas directive, currently under discussion, and on movement towards third party access to pipelines throughout Europe.

The decision to base the contract at the National Balancing Point -- a notional point on the national pipeline grid after gas has had entry charges applied to enter the system -- rather than at the main landing terminal of Bacton is due partly to recent growth of NBP trade on the spot market. But it also reflects continued problems in verifying that gas said to have been delivered at Bacton has actually been handed over. This verification process, handled by the Claims Validation Agent (CVA), has dogged the launch of the contract more than any other single factor.

"Bacton trade is declining slightly", said Ward, "and NBP trade is growing. But Bacton is still important and we will continue to develop a contract there". He added that the IPE will aim to be responsive to market conditions in deciding when or whether to introduce contracts at other terminals or for other time periods at some future date, but no decisions have been reached yet.
